content: The MMR vaccine is a combination of live attenuated viruses administered via injection to provide immunization against measles, mumps, and rubella. It has been widely used globally since its introduction in the 1970s, with over 500 million doses administered in more than 60 countries. In the United States, a booster dose was introduced in the mid-1990s. As with all vaccines, the long-term effects and efficacy of the MMR vaccine continue to be studied. The vaccine is marketed under different names by various manufacturers, including M-M-R II by Merck, Priorix by GlaxoSmithKline, and TRIMOVAX by Sanofi Pasteur. Before the widespread use of the measles vaccine, the disease was so prevalent that infection was considered inevitable. Today, in countries with routine childhood vaccination programs, the incidence of measles has dropped to less than 1% among individuals under 30 years of age. Vaccination has been shown to prevent illness, disability, and death associated with measles. For example, in the United States, vaccination has prevented an estimated 52 million cases of measles, 17,400 cases of mental retardation, and 5,200 deaths. Globally, measles remains endemic, but vaccination efforts have significantly reduced mortality rates. Mumps, another viral disease of childhood, was once very common. A rare but known complication of mumps is male sterility. Rubella, also known as German measles, was similarly widespread before vaccination. The primary risk of rubella is its potential to cause congenital rubella syndrome in babies if a pregnant woman becomes infected, leading to severe congenital defects. All three diseases are highly contagious. The combined MMR vaccine was developed to provide immunity more efficiently and with less discomfort than administering three separate injections. In 2005, the Cochrane Library reviewed 31 scientific studies on the MMR vaccine. While the review noted the significant impact of mass immunization on disease elimination, it found no studies meeting its inclusion criteria to assess the vaccine's effectiveness. The authors concluded that existing evidence supports the safety and efficacy of the MMR vaccine and current policies of mass immunization aimed at reducing morbidity and mortality associated with measles, mumps, and rubella. The viral strains used in the MMR vaccine were developed through propagation in animal and human cells. For example, the mumps and measles virus strains were grown in embryonated hens' eggs and chick embryo cell cultures, producing attenuated strains less virulent to human cells. The rubella component, Meruvax, is propagated using a human cell line (WI-38) derived from embryonic lung tissue in 1961. The use of human cell lines has led to some religious controversy. The vaccine is supplied in a freeze-dried form and reconstituted with a provided solvent before subcutaneous injection. High vaccination coverage before the age of two is critical, and a second booster dose is necessary to achieve satisfactory immunity levels and interrupt virus transmission. The booster can be administered as early as one month after the first dose. Adverse reactions to the MMR vaccine are generally mild and rarely serious. Approximately 10% of children develop fever, malaise, and rash 5–21 days after the first dose, and 5% experience temporary joint pain. Older women are at higher risk of joint pain, acute arthritis, and, rarely, chronic arthritis. Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, is extremely rare. Reports of neurological disorders are minimal, except for an association between the Urabe mumps strain in some MMR vaccines and rare cases of aseptic meningitis, a mild and transient form of viral meningitis. Due to these cases, the UK National Health Service stopped using the Urabe strain in the early 1990s, switching to the Jeryl Lynn mumps strain. However, the Urabe strain remains in use in some countries due to its lower manufacturing cost and higher efficacy, despite a slightly higher rate of mild side effects. The Cochrane Library review identified several issues with the quality of MMR vaccine safety studies and recommended adopting standardized definitions of adverse events. The review concluded that the evidence of adverse events cannot be separated from the vaccine's role in preventing the target diseases. In the UK, the MMR vaccine became controversial following a 1998 paper by Andrew Wakefield and colleagues, which reported a study of 12 children with autism spectrum disorders and bowel symptoms, many of whom developed symptoms shortly after receiving the MMR vaccine. During a press conference, Wakefield suggested that administering the vaccines in three separate doses might be safer, although this suggestion was not supported by the study. Subsequent peer-reviewed studies have found no association between the MMR vaccine and autism. Administering the vaccines separately does not reduce adverse effects and increases the risk of infection from diseases not yet immunized against. Wakefield has been heavily criticized for his research methods and for contributing to a decline in vaccination rates. In 2004, ten of Wakefield's twelve coauthors formally retracted the interpretation section of the study. Major health organizations, including the Centers for Disease Control, the Institute of Medicine, the UK National Health Service, and the Cochrane Library, have all concluded that there is no evidence linking the MMR vaccine to autism. The MMRV vaccine, which combines the MMR vaccine with the varicella (chickenpox) vaccine, has been proposed as a replacement for the MMR vaccine to simplify vaccine administration.
